title: New York auditions, Harlem clubs and the Paris engagement as La Rose Noire
summary: She worked at Dash's Inn and the Capitol on Lenox Avenue, then went to Paris with Danny Wilson and Ali Laguerre. There she worked at Chez Michels and became La Rose Noire.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: if I was gonna make any money, you know. And so he told me, well, the idea was he had the telegram. He showed me the telegram from the Victor in the Columbia, telling him to bring a blues singer for audition, you know. And so he said, I would get all my transportation paid and everything, and I told him, could I get an advance? I wanted to make sure. So he said, yes, he asked me what I wanted, I told him. And so then I said, well, I'd go, and I went to New York and made a test for the Columbia and the OK, and Jimmy McHugh of the Mills staff, music staff, taking me to the Victor and played my first test on the Victor, dear old Southland. He wanted them to hear me, hear my voice, you know. And he figured that that would be the song to sing so they could see the volume of my voice and so on. Then Russell Robertson, piano player, I think he's out of Memphis. And he was working hard to get me the job as blues singer with the Blackbirds. But it was one of those things where, you know, it's like we say politics. And this Perry Bradford who had discovered Mamie Smith, he was then working on Edith Wilson. And so he got Edith Wilson in there, you see. Russell, he told me all how it was done and everything, you know. So then that's how Edith Wilson got the job in with Blackbirds. And then I start working around the nightclubs in New York. My first nightclub in New York was out at a place called Dash's Inn. It was opening up for Easter. And I got in town just about the time for the grand opening. And so they wanted a new face, you know. They didn't want anybody around town. And so I happened to be stopping with Lucille Hegeman, a blues singer you might know of her. Her husband was a piano player, Hegeman. He had a band. I think he, but when he took his band to Japan, I don't think he ever came back. I think he stayed over there. And last we heard, he had married a Japanese girl over there, and had raised a family and stayed over there and never came back. Well, they are the ones who recommended me to this Dash's Inn. And that's when I started working. While I was working there, I got an offer then to come to a, there was a man gonna see how a big cabaret would go in New York, you know, in Harlem. They had all those small places, you know, little small. And he opened a place that was a block long, the capital on Lenox Avenue between 139 and 40, I think it was. So naturally, he was out scouting around to get all the new talent he could. And his manager, assistant manager came where I was working, started talking to me about coming to work there. Then that was right in the heart of Harlem. So then they offered me a nice salary, and I left where I was at and went there. Well, I worked there, I guess, about three years. And that's where I left. Then Billy Pierce then was starting to book people for Paris, for the Moulin Rouge. And he had a bunch of girls he had booked up to go. And he said, you want to see if I want to go. And well, I told him, no, I wasn't interested in no theater work. And so then there was an entertainer who I had worked with, who went to Paris, Bricktop. And she was writing letters back of all the money she was making, you know. And so, well, I knew if Bricktop was making that kind of money, well, I had to say brag it on myself. I knew I was a better singer than her. So I figured I want to go there and get some of that money too. So then I was talking to the band and the piano player, Danny Wilson, maybe you know of him. He wrote that piece, With Someone Like You Around Me, How Could I Feel Blue? Beautiful number it is. Well, he said, I think I'll go over there. Then there was a saxophone and violin player, Ali Laguerre. He said, well, maybe I'll make the trip. I said, well, why not the three of us get together and we go together and we stick together and we look for work over there. It'll be us three. So that's how we planned it. And we said, okay. So we put our hands together and we did. And we left on the France, on the French liner, France or Paris, I think, one of the French boats anyway. We left and we went to Paris. And we happened to get in there just when a place was going to open up. Mrs. Regina Buchen, she was opening up a nightclub. And there was an American from America named Louis Mitchell. He was going to be in charge of the place, you see. And most all of those French places over there at that time, they would have American, they had American, you know, musicians and entertainers. And they would have the place named after them because they'd done the interpreting with the customers, you see. So they named the place Chez Michels, you see. But he was just the manager, you know, same way as they had a place named Chez Florence. Well, Florence Jones and her husband Palmer Jones were the entertainers there, you see. But it was a French woman who owned the place. And Bricktop, then she was working at, on Rue Pigalle. And they call it Chez Bricktop, you see. But she was working for a Frenchman, too. So then I went in there with myself, Danny Wilson, and Lily Gare. We went in there at this place, Chez Michels, you see. But it seems as though he had, he was with the place where Florence was. And this woman thought that he was going to, you know, take all the business away from there and come there, but it seems as though he didn't draw as well as she thought he was going to. So then she let him go and took in a troop of Russians. Alexander Storzynski and a troop of Russians. And in this troop, there was two, do the Russians have princes and prince? Well, there was two princes and two prince that was singing in the chorus. And they used to just talk my head off back there about America. And, oh, how they would love to come to America. And then they compared our salary with the salary they was getting over there. You see, we were getting double to what they got, you know. And so that's where I got the name of the Black Rose and La Rose Noire. And they had black satin roses that would give to each customer, you see. And when they'd introduce me, they would introduce me as La Rose Noire, you know, the Black Rose. And I was then doing a couple of Sidney Bechet's number, Do That Thing. And in this song, it said something about poke chops. So those people, all they could say was poke chops when they wanted the song. They said, sing poke chop, poke chop. Oh, so... Well, okay, let's see what we're going to do.
